analogy.p: Think of breaking bonds as paying money out of your account (you must spend energy) and making bonds as being paid wages into it. If your wages (bonds made) are bigger than your spending (bonds broken) your balance rises and the extra is given to the surroundings as heat: exothermic. If you spend more than you earn you must take energy from the surroundings: endothermic. The analogy breaks down because real bond energies are averages and the 'payment' happens at the same time as the 'spending', not one after the other.

bullets: **Break bonds = endothermic** (energy taken in from the surroundings).
**Make bonds = exothermic** (energy released to the surroundings).
**Overall energy change = energy needed to break bonds - energy released making bonds.**
You must also **decide whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic** from the sign of your answer and explain it.
The bond energies are **normally given**, but you must pick the right ones and multiply by the correct number of bonds.
This builds on reaction profiles (Energy changes > Reaction profiles) and on covalent bonding from Topic 2.
core.h: What the specification asks (Higher tier only)
core.p: AQA expects you to **calculate the overall energy change of a reaction from bond energies**. During any chemical reaction, **energy must be supplied to break the bonds in the reactants** and **energy is released when new bonds form in the products**. The overall energy change is the **difference** between those two totals. This is a Higher tier skill, so it appears as a 3 to 5 mark calculation on Paper 1, usually with the bond energies given in a table.

bullets: Breaking a bond is **always endothermic**, whatever the reaction.
Forming a bond is **always exothermic**, whatever the reaction.
A reaction is a competition: which is bigger, **total energy in** or **total energy out**?
The energy to break a bond and the energy released on forming it are **equal in size** for the same bond (for example H-H is 436 kJ/mol both ways).
This is conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings.
Common wrong idea: 'exothermic reactions do not break bonds'. They do, but they release **more** energy forming new bonds than they spend breaking old ones.
core.h: Why bond breaking takes in energy and bond making releases it
core.p: Atoms in a covalent bond are held together by the electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the two positive nuclei. To pull the atoms apart you must do work against that attraction, so energy is **taken in** from the surroundings. When atoms come together to form a bond they move into a lower energy, more stable arrangement and the energy difference is **released**, usually as heat. The same bond releases exactly as much energy when it forms as it needs to break.

bullets: Unit: **kJ/mol**. The answer to a bond energy calculation is also in **kJ/mol**.
Typical values: H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 432, C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O-H 464, N-H 391, N≡N 945, C-C 347 (kJ/mol). Do not memorise; they are given in the exam.
**Multiple bonds are stronger**: C-C (347) < C=C (about 612) < C≡C (about 838), because more shared electron pairs hold the nuclei together.
**Short bonds are generally stronger** than long bonds between the same type of atoms.
Bond energy is a property of **covalent bonds**; do not use these calculations for ionic lattices.
The values assume all substances are **gases**; changes of state (such as steam condensing to liquid water) add extra energy that is not included.
core.h: Bond energy: definition, units and what the size tells you
core.p: **Bond energy** is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, and it is measured in **kJ/mol** (kilojoules per mole). A **large** bond energy means a **strong** bond that takes a lot of energy to break. Because the same bond type appears in many molecules, the values used are **average** bond energies, so calculated answers are close to, not exactly equal to, experimental values.

bullets: **Step 1:** write the balanced symbol equation and draw **displayed formulae** (every bond shown as a line).
**Step 2:** list the bonds in the **reactants** and multiply each by how many times it occurs (include the balancing numbers).
**Step 3:** add them to get **energy needed to break bonds** (energy in), in kJ/mol.
**Step 4:** list the bonds in the **products**, multiply by their numbers, and add to get **energy released making bonds** (energy out).
**Step 5:** overall energy change = **energy in - energy out**.
**Step 6:** state the sign: **negative = exothermic**, **positive = endothermic**, and write the unit kJ/mol.
Check: if energy out is bigger than energy in, your answer must be negative. If not, you have subtracted the wrong way round.
core.p: Always follow the same layout so you gain method marks even if you slip on arithmetic. Start from a **balanced** equation, draw out every molecule so you can see each bond, then add up energy in and energy out separately before subtracting. Show every line of working because AQA mark schemes award marks for the correct sum of bonds broken, the correct sum of bonds made and the correct subtraction.

bullets: **H2**: one H-H bond. **Cl2**: one Cl-Cl bond. **O2**: one **O=O** (double) bond. **N2**: one **N≡N** (triple) bond.
**HCl**: one H-Cl bond. **H2O**: **two** O-H bonds. **NH3**: **three** N-H bonds. **CH4**: **four** C-H bonds.
**CO2** (O=C=O): **two** C=O bonds.
**Ethane C2H6**: one C-C and six C-H bonds. **Ethene C2H4**: one C=C and four C-H bonds.
**Methanol CH3OH**: three C-H, one C-O, one O-H bonds.
Total bonds for 2H2O = 2 x 2 = **4 O-H bonds**; for 3H2 = **3 H-H bonds**.

Bonds that stay the same on both sides (for example a C-H bond that is unchanged) are in practice **broken and remade in this method**, which gives the same answer as ignoring them. Use whichever your question demands, but be consistent.
core.h: Counting bonds correctly from displayed formulae
core.p: The commonest source of lost marks is counting bonds wrongly. Look at the **displayed formula** of each molecule and count every line; a double bond is **one C=O bond** with its own energy value, not two C-O bonds. Then multiply by the **balancing number** in front of the formula, because 2H2O means two molecules each with two O-H bonds, giving four O-H bonds.

bullets: **Exothermic:** energy out (bonds made) **>** energy in (bonds broken). ΔH is **negative**.
**Endothermic:** energy in (bonds broken) **>** energy out (bonds made). ΔH is **positive**.
ΔH is for the equation **as written**: doubling the equation doubles the value.
Reversing the reaction **changes the sign** but not the size (for example +185 becomes -185).
Typical exothermic reactions: combustion, neutralisation, many oxidations. Typical endothermic: thermal decomposition, photosynthesis.
**Use correct wording**: 'more energy is released when bonds form than is needed to break bonds' earns the explanation mark.
core.h: Interpreting the answer: sign, size and meaning
core.p: The sign of the answer tells you the type of reaction. A **negative** value means more energy was released forming bonds than was taken in breaking them, so energy is transferred **to the surroundings**: the reaction is **exothermic** and the surroundings get **hotter**. A **positive** value means the opposite: the reaction is **endothermic** and the surroundings get **colder**. The size of the number tells you how much energy per mole of the reaction as written.

bullets: Bonds broken: **1 x H-H + 1 x Cl-Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ/mol**.
Bonds made: **2 x H-Cl = 2 x 432 = 864 kJ/mol**.
Conclusion: **exothermic**, because more energy is released making the two H-Cl bonds than is needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl.
The experimental value is close to -184 kJ/mol, showing the average bond energies work well.
Notice the arithmetic order: **in minus out**. Writing out minus in gives +185 and the wrong conclusion.
core.p: This is the classic example. In the reactants there is one H-H bond (436 kJ/mol) and one Cl-Cl bond (243 kJ/mol). In the products there are two H-Cl bonds (432 kJ/mol each). Energy in is 436 + 243 = **679 kJ/mol**. Energy out is 2 x 432 = **864 kJ/mol**. The overall change is 679 - 864 = **-185 kJ/mol**, so the reaction is exothermic.

bullets: Overall energy change = **energy of products - energy of reactants** on the profile.
Bond energies tell you the **size of the gap** between reactant and product levels.
The peak height (activation energy) is **not** found from bond energy tables at GCSE.
Activation energy is not the same as the total energy to break every bond: bond breaking and bond making overlap as the reaction proceeds.
A catalyst lowers the **activation energy** but does **not** change the overall energy change.
Exothermic: arrow on the profile points **down**; endothermic: arrow points **up**.
core.h: Link to reaction profiles and activation energy
core.p: A reaction profile plots energy against progress of reaction. For an exothermic reaction the products sit **lower** than the reactants, and the gap is the overall energy change. The **activation energy** is the minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to happen, shown by the height of the peak above the reactants. The bond energy calculation gives only the **overall energy change**, not the activation energy.

bullets: Energy out = **6x** because 2NH3 contains **six** N-H bonds.
Equation: 2253 - 6x = -93.
Rearrange: 6x = 2253 + 93 = 2346, so x = **391 kJ/mol**.
Always check by substituting back: 2253 - 6 x 391 = 2253 - 2346 = -93. ✓
The same skill can be used for an unknown bond in the reactants: rearrange for energy in first.
core.h: Working backwards: finding an unknown bond energy
core.p: Exam questions sometimes give the overall energy change and ask for one unknown bond energy. Write the same equation, but with the unknown as x, set energy in minus energy out equal to the given ΔH, then rearrange. For example for N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 with ΔH = -93 kJ/mol, N≡N = 945 and H-H = 436, the N-H bond energy x satisfies (945 + 3 x 436) - 6x = -93.

bullets: Average bond energies differ slightly from the true value in a specific molecule.
The calculation assumes **all substances are gases**; real reactions may involve liquids.
Experimental values (for example from burning a fuel under a calorimeter) include **heat loss** and incomplete combustion, so they are usually less than the theoretical value.
Strong agreement between calculation and experiment supports the idea that **energy changes are due to bond breaking and making**.
When asked to 'suggest why the calculated and experimental values differ', mention **average bond energies** and **heat loss to the surroundings**.
Never say the calculation is 'wrong'; say it is 'an approximation'.
core.h: Why the answers are only approximate
core.p: Bond energies in data tables are **average** values taken over many different molecules, but the real energy needed to break a bond depends slightly on the other atoms around it. The method also assumes everything is a gas and ignores changes of state. So the answer is a good estimate of the energy change, not an exact measurement. You can compare it with a value found by experiment (for example using calorimetry) to evaluate the method.

bullets: Use the **balanced** equation; unbalanced equations give the wrong number of bonds.
Multiply **bond energy x number of bonds**, not just list the values.
**Bonds in molecules like CO2** count twice (two C=O bonds).
**Subtract in the right order: in - out.** The sign is the final check.
Keep the unit **kJ/mol** with every total and the final answer.
Do not mix up **bond energy values** with **activation energy** values.
Do not 'cancel' bonds that appear on both sides unless the question tells you to.
core.p: Most errors are not conceptual but procedural. Using an unbalanced equation, forgetting to multiply by the balancing number, or confusing the sign convention will cost marks. Use a table with columns for bond, number, energy per bond and total, then total each side. This keeps the working neat and allows error-carried-forward marks.

bullets: **Exothermic:** temperature of surroundings **rises**; products have **less** energy; ΔH **negative**; e.g. burning methane, neutralisation, respiration.

**Endothermic:** temperature of surroundings **falls**; products have **more** energy; ΔH **positive**; e.g. thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, photosynthesis, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate.
Everyday uses: **hand warmers** (exothermic), **cold packs** (endothermic).
Fuels: the large negative ΔH of combustion is why hydrocarbons are good fuels.
Higher link: bond calculations support the idea that the **chemical energy store** changes as bonds change.
Link to rates: reactions need **activation energy** whether they are exothermic or endothermic.
core.h: Exothermic and endothermic reactions compared, with examples
core.p: Putting the two types side by side helps you remember the energy bookkeeping. In both cases bonds are broken and made; the only difference is which total is larger. This is also the link between what you measure (temperature change) and what is happening in the particles (energy transfer in bond changes).

exam: **Command words:** 'Calculate' means show the working and finish with units; 'Explain' means link the sign of the answer to energy in and energy out; 'Deduce' means use the number to decide exothermic or endothermic.
**Typical marks:** a full bond energy calculation is usually **3 to 5 marks**: 1 for energy in, 1 for energy out, 1 for subtraction and sign, plus marks for correct units and conclusion.
**Model phrase:** 'Energy is needed to break bonds (endothermic) and energy is released when bonds form (exothermic). More energy is released than taken in, so the reaction is exothermic.'
**Always show working:** write bonds broken, bonds made, and the subtraction on separate lines, because error carried forward marks are available.
**Check the sign** against the story: if energy out is larger, the answer must be negative.
**Use the data table:** only use the bond energies given; do not use values from memory if they differ.
**1 mark:** 'Bond breaking is endothermic'. **2 marks:** state what is broken and what is made, then compare the totals.
**Unknown bond energy questions:** set up an equation with x, and rearrange; check by substitution.
**Link to reaction profile:** if asked to sketch, show products lower than reactants for exothermic and label the overall energy change and activation energy.
**Evaluate:** say average bond energies and heat loss cause differences between calculated and experimental values.

mistakes.r: Overall energy change = energy needed to break bonds - energy released making bonds (in - out).
mistakes.w: Energy change = energy released - energy needed.

mistakes.r: 2H2O has four O-H bonds; multiply the bond energy by the total number of that bond.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply by the balancing number.

mistakes.r: CO2 (O=C=O) has two C=O double bonds.
mistakes.w: Counting CO2 as one bond or C-O bonds.

mistakes.r: Bonds are broken in every reaction; exothermic reactions release more energy forming bonds than they need to break bonds.
mistakes.w: Exothermic reactions do not break any bonds.

mistakes.r: Positive ΔH means endothermic; negative ΔH means exothermic.
Bond breaking takes in energy (endothermic); bond making releases energy (exothermic).
Balance the equation first, then count bonds.
It gives only the overall energy change; the activation energy is shown on a reaction profile.
mistakes.w: Bond energy calculation gives the activation energy.

summary: Higher tier: calculate the overall energy change of a reaction by subtracting the energy released when new bonds form from the energy needed to break the old bonds, using bond energies in kJ/mol, then use the sign to decide whether it is exothermic or endothermic. It matters because it links particle-level bond changes to the energy transfers you can measure.

Energy needed to break bonds in the reactants minus energy released when bonds form in the products.

worked.ans: -185 kJ/mol; exothermic, because more energy is released making H-Cl bonds (864) than is needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl (679).
worked.q: Use the bond energies H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 432 (kJ/mol) to calculate the overall energy change for H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. State whether it is exothermic or endothermic. (4 marks)
steps: Bonds broken: 1 x H-H + 1 x Cl-Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ/mol.
Bonds made: 2 x H-Cl = 2 x 432 = 864 kJ/mol.
Overall energy change = energy in - energy out = 679 - 864 = -185 kJ/mol.
Negative value, so energy is released to the surroundings.

worked.ans: -818 kJ/mol; exothermic (energy out is greater than energy in).
worked.q: Calculate the overall energy change for CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O using C-H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O-H 464 (kJ/mol). (5 marks)
steps: Bonds broken: 4 x C-H = 4 x 413 = 1652; 2 x O=O = 2 x 498 = 996.
Bonds made: 2 x C=O = 2 x 805 = 1610; 2 molecules H2O each 2 O-H = 4 x 464 = 1856.
